title: Quantum Information Decoupling Beyond Finite Dimensions
authors: Hayata Yamasaki
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26123v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum information decoupling is a pillar of quantum information theory, underlying quantum communication, error correction, and information recovery. However, its existing formulations rely on random unitary operations tied to finite-dimensional assumptions on quantum systems. Here we establish a decoupling framework for arbitrary separable, possibly infinite-dimensional systems. For finite-dimensional inputs and arbitrary separable reference/output systems, we derive error bounds on one-shot decoupling for completely positive maps in terms of sandwiched R\'enyi conditional entropies. For partial-trace decoupling with finite-dimensional references, the error exponent is optimal up to the known critical rate. To handle infinite-dimensional inputs, we assume finite entropy of the manipulated system. We construct finite-rank projections on independent and identically distributed (IID) states to restrict randomization to a projected finite-dimensional subspace, while ensuring high success probability by including auxiliary components in the discarded subsystem at asymptotically negligible cost. This leads to an infinite-dimensional IID partial-trace decoupling protocol achieving optimal asymptotic dimension rates. As an application, we construct an infinite-dimensional quantum-state-merging protocol, a mother protocol of quantum information theory. Under finite entropy of Alice's marginal, it achieves the same quantum-communication and total-cost rates as in finite dimensions, governed by mutual information and conditional entropy. These results show that the operational interpretation of entropic quantities through these achievable rates constitutes a universal principle beyond finite dimensions. More broadly, our framework provides foundational tools for exploring quantum information regardless of whether we model the physical world using finite- or infinite-dimensional spaces.
tldr: Establishes a quantum information decoupling framework for infinite-dimensional systems, achieving optimal rates and enabling quantum-state merging beyond finite dimensions.
motivation: Existing decoupling formulations rely on finite-dimensional assumptions, limiting applicability to realistic infinite-dimensional systems like continuous-variable quantum optics.
method: Derives one-shot decoupling error bounds using sandwiched Rényi conditional entropies for finite-dimensional inputs, and constructs finite-rank projections on IID states to handle infinite-dimensional inputs while ensuring high success probability.
result: Achieves optimal asymptotic dimension rates for infinite-dimensional IID partial-trace decoupling, and extends quantum-state merging to infinite dimensions with the same rates as finite dimensions under finite entropy conditions.
conclusion: The operational interpretation of entropic quantities through achievable rates is a universal principle beyond finite dimensions, providing foundational tools for quantum information in arbitrary separable spaces.

title: Qubit-qubit-qutrit Quantum Correlations In $h \to F \bar F V$
authors: Micha{\l} Banacki, Misaki Ohta, Abhyoudai S. Shaleena, Pawe{\l} Caban, Micha{\l} Eckstein, Kazuki Sakurai, Michael Spannowsky, Pawe{\l} Horodecki
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26122v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We perform an extensive analysis of the quantum correlations carried by the qubit-qubit-qutrit pure state arising in the decay of a massive scalar into a fermion-antifermion pair and a massive gauge boson, [MATH], specialising to the Higgs boson decay [MATH]. Working with the exact tree-level spin state and its systematic expansion around the massless-fermion limit, we obtain analytic control over the entire phase space: the bipartite entanglement measures, the genuine [MATH] entanglement structure (the Miyake classification), as well as the Bell-inequality violations and the non-stabiliserness (magic) are all mapped and reproduced by compact formulas. The bipartite measures exhibit a monogamy-like trade-off between the fermion pair and the fermion-boson pairs. The state is genuinely [MATH] entangled over almost the entire phase space, most strongly in the collinear regions. We derive, for the first time, semi-analytical expressions for the tight [MATH] Bell inequalities of the [MATH] system, generalising the optimisation previously available only for three qubits, and find that the local-hidden-variable bound is violated over the entire phase space, reaching within a few per cent of the quantum bound at the upper endpoint of the di-tau mass spectrum. We further extend the stabiliser R\'enyi entropy and the non-local magic to systems with unequal local dimensions, and show that the near-endpoint state carries almost exactly one bit of non-local magic, which peaks at [MATH] in the collinear regions. The differential decay rate concentrates precisely in the most nonclassical region of the phase space.
tldr: This paper analyzes quantum correlations in a qubit-qubit-qutrit state from Higgs decay, mapping entanglement, Bell violations, and magic across phase space.
motivation: Understanding quantum correlations in high-energy particle decays can reveal fundamental aspects of quantum information in nature and test nonclassicality.
method: Using exact tree-level spin states and systematic expansions, the authors compute bipartite entanglement measures, genuine tripartite entanglement classification, Bell inequalities, and stabilizer Rényi entropy for the mixed-dimensional system.
result: The state is genuinely tripartite entangled over almost all phase space, violates Bell inequalities everywhere, and carries up to one bit of non-local magic, with the differential decay rate peaking in the most nonclassical region.
conclusion: Higgs boson decay provides a rich platform for studying quantum correlations in mixed-dimensional systems, with potential applications to quantum information processing and tests of fundamental physics.

The authors work with the exact tree-level spin state and develop a systematic expansion around the massless-fermion limit, enabling analytic control over the entire phase space. They map bipartite entanglement measures, genuine 2⊗2⊗3 entanglement structure (Miyake classification), Bell-inequality violations, and non-stabiliserness (magic) using compact formulas. The bipartite measures reveal a monogamy-like trade-off between the fermion pair and fermion-boson pairs. The authors derive semi-analytical expressions for tight 4×4×2 Bell inequalities for the 2⊗2⊗3 system, generalizing previous optimization for three qubits, and find violations over the entire phase space, reaching within a few percent of the quantum bound at the upper endpoint of the di-tau mass spectrum. For genuine tripartite entanglement, they use the Miyake classification for 2⊗2⊗3 systems, which involves checking the positivity of partial transposes across different bipartitions. title: Contextual Advantage Implies Limited Distinguishability In Any Physical Theory
authors: Roberto D. Baldij\~{a}o, Felipe A. Barretto, Jaros\l{}aw K. Korbicz
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26145v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A central question in quantum information is whether a given set of states can provide an advantage in some information-processing task. We establish a universal connection between two such questions: how well a set of states can be discriminated, and whether it can power tasks whose advantage stems from generalized contextuality. Working in the framework of generalized probabilistic theories (GPTs), which includes quantum and classical systems as special cases, we show that any set of states able to provide a nonclassical advantage in a contextuality-powered task must obey nontrivial upper bounds on the success probability of every state discrimination task using the full set. Contextual advantage therefore implies limited distinguishability, exposing a trade-off between two basic operational resources. Importantly, this is more than a statement about the idealized limit: perfect distinguishability is not needed to preclude contextuality. Our thresholds lie strictly below unity, so any set whose discrimination performance exceeds them while still imperfectly distinguishable is already guaranteed to admit a noncontextual explanation. The bounds follow from a simple geometric property, linear dependence of the state set, take a closed analytical form, and depend only on the prior of the task and the convex geometry of the states. As an illustration, we apply them to generalized parity-oblivious multiplexing, where sufficiently high success in the task implies that at least one sub-ensemble of the codebook cannot power any contextual advantage.
tldr: Establishes a universal trade-off between contextual advantage and state distinguishability in any generalized probabilistic theory.
motivation: To understand the relationship between two fundamental operational resources: the ability of a set of states to provide a nonclassical advantage in contextuality-powered tasks and their distinguishability.
method: Uses the framework of generalized probabilistic theories (GPTs) and derives bounds on state discrimination success probability from the linear dependence of the state set, a geometric property.
result: Any set of states that can provide a contextual advantage must have limited distinguishability, with explicit thresholds below unity that depend only on the prior and convex geometry.
conclusion: Contextual advantage implies limited distinguishability, revealing a fundamental trade-off and providing a necessary condition for noncontextual explanations.

This reveals a trade-off between two basic operational resources: contextual advantage and state distinguishability. Importantly, the bounds are strict—they lie below unity—meaning that perfect distinguishability is not required to preclude contextuality; even imperfectly distinguishable sets that exceed the bound are guaranteed to admit a noncontextual explanation. The bounds follow from a simple geometric property: linear dependence of the state set. deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors work within the framework of generalized probabilistic theories (GPTs), which allows them to treat quantum and classical systems on equal footing. They define contextuality in terms of operational equivalence and noncontextual ontological models, following the approach of Spekkens. The key technical tool is the concept of linear dependence of the state set: a set of states is linearly dependent if one state can be expressed as an affine combination of the others. The authors show that if a set of states can provide a contextual advantage, then the states must be linearly dependent. From this, they derive upper bounds on the success probability of any state discrimination task using the full set. The bounds are expressed in terms of the prior probabilities and the convex geometry of the state space. The derivation is rigorous and uses only basic convex geometry and linear algebra, making the results widely accessible.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main result is a set of inequalities that bound the maximum success probability for state discrimination given a set of states that can exhibit contextual advantage. Specifically, for a set of states {ρ_i} with prior probabilities p_i, the success probability P_success satisfies P_success ≤ 1 - (1/2) * (1 - max_i p_i) * (something related to linear dependence). The exact bound depends on the specific linear dependence relation. The authors show that these bounds are tight in some cases. For example, in the case of two states, the bound reduces to the well-known fact that nonorthogonal states cannot be perfectly discriminated. The application to generalized parity-oblivious multiplexing shows that if the success probability exceeds a certain threshold, then at least one sub-ensemble of the codebook cannot be used for contextual advantage. The paper does not provide explicit numerical values for the bounds in general, but the analytical form is given.

title: Graph Theoretic Approach To Quantum Nonstabilizerness
authors: Yingjian Liu, Albert Gasull, Mengyao Hu, Ruiyun Zhang, Flavio Baccari, Jordi Tura
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Detecting nonstabilizerness requires full tomography and an optimization over exponentially many stabilizer states. A limited Pauli measurement set promises resource-efficient magic certification, yet the resulting reduced stabilizer polytope is generally difficult to characterize. We trace this difficulty into two coupled obstructions: the simultaneous measurability of measurements captured by their frustration graph structure, and the consistency of sign dependencies from stabilizer formalism. We show that the sign dependencies can be discarded exactly whenever active dependencies are absent, and that perfect frustration graphs then make this reduced polytope efficiently solvable. This solvable regime derives a closed form bounded by the clique number of the frustration graph, revealing a tradeoff between witness capacity and simultaneous measurability. Clifford covariance allows rotated measurement sets to enlarge the detectable state space without raising the capacity. Graph structure therefore emerges as both a certificate of tractability and a design principle for scalable magic resource detection.
tldr: This paper introduces a graph-theoretic framework for efficient detection of nonstabilizerness (magic) in quantum states using limited Pauli measurements.
motivation: Detecting nonstabilizerness is crucial for quantum computing but requires full tomography; the authors aim to reduce complexity by using a limited set of Pauli measurements.
method: They model simultaneous measurability via frustration graphs and show that when sign dependencies are absent and the graph is perfect, the reduced stabilizer polytope becomes efficiently solvable, yielding a closed-form bound based on the clique number.
result: The frustration graph structure determines tractability and provides a tradeoff between witness capacity and simultaneous measurability; Clifford covariance can enlarge detectable states without increasing capacity.
conclusion: Graph structure serves as both a certificate of tractability and a design principle for scalable magic resource detection.

It identifies two coupled obstructions: the simultaneous measurability of Pauli measurements, captured by their frustration graph structure, and the consistency of sign dependencies from stabilizer formalism. The authors show that when active sign dependencies are absent and the frustration graph is perfect, the reduced stabilizer polytope becomes efficiently solvable, yielding a closed-form bound on magic witness capacity given by the clique number of the frustration graph. This reveals a tradeoff between witness capacity and simultaneous measurability. Clifford covariance allows rotated measurement sets to enlarge the detectable state space without increasing capacity. The work establishes graph structure as both a certificate of tractability and a design principle for scalable magic resource detection.

Proof that discarding sign dependencies is exact when active dependencies are absent, and that perfect frustration graphs make the reduced polytope efficiently solvable.
Derivation of a closed-form bound on witness capacity given by the clique number of the frustration graph, revealing a tradeoff between capacity and simultaneous measurability.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a graph-theoretic approach to characterize the reduced stabilizer polytope arising from a limited set of Pauli measurements. The frustration graph encodes which measurements are not simultaneously measurable, and the sign dependencies are analyzed via stabilizer formalism. The authors prove that when the frustration graph is perfect and no active sign dependencies exist, the polytope's extreme points correspond to stabilizer states consistent with the measurement set, and the witness capacity is bounded by the clique number. Clifford covariance is used to rotate measurement sets, expanding the detectable region without increasing the bound. The analysis is theoretical, relying on convex geometry and graph theory, with no numerical simulations reported.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is a closed-form expression for the maximum magic witness value achievable with a given measurement set: it equals the clique number of the frustration graph. The paper also shows that Clifford rotations can map different measurement sets to each other, allowing the detectable state space to be enlarged without increasing the clique number. No specific numerical values are given, but the bound is exact for perfect graphs. The results are analytical and apply to any number of qubits, though the perfect graph condition may be restrictive.

title: Algebraic Paradoxes In Adaptive Quantum Computation
authors: Samson Abramsky, Rui Soares Barbosa, Carmen Constantin, Martti Karvonen
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26157v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC) is a universal model of quantum computation whose full power requires adaptivity. Contextuality is known to power quantum advantage in MBQC, yet it has resisted algebraic analysis in the adaptive setting. We show that if an adaptive [MATH]-linear measurement-based quantum computing protocol deterministically computes a non-affine Boolean function, then the underlying quantum resource satisfies an inconsistent set of linear equations. This witnesses an algebraic form of strong contextuality generalising Mermin's All-versus-Nothing arguments. Such algebraic contextuality can be detected cohomologically, resolving an open question posed by Raussendorf, who had established cohomological witnesses of contextuality for non-adaptive protocols, but left the adaptive case open. We prove this result constructively: we model adaptive measurement protocols as ordinary measurements on a larger scenario of tree-like measurements, and explicitly build the inconsistent equations inductively.
tldr: This paper shows that adaptive measurement-based quantum computing protocols deterministically computing non-affine Boolean functions imply an inconsistent set of linear equations, revealing algebraic contextuality.
motivation: Contextuality is known to power quantum advantage in MBQC, but its algebraic analysis in the adaptive setting was missing. The authors aim to extend cohomological contextuality detection to adaptive protocols.
method: They model adaptive measurement protocols as ordinary measurements on a larger scenario of tree-like measurements and construct inconsistent linear equations inductively.
result: They prove that adaptive MBQC protocols computing non-affine functions witness an algebraic form of strong contextuality generalizing Mermin's All-versus-Nothing arguments, detectable cohomologically.
conclusion: This resolves an open question by Raussendorf, providing a cohomological witness of contextuality for adaptive protocols, deepening the understanding of quantum advantage in MBQC.

The authors prove that if an adaptive Z2-linear MBQC protocol deterministically computes a non-affine Boolean function, then the underlying quantum resource (e.g., a graph state) must satisfy an inconsistent set of linear equations. This inconsistency serves as a witness of contextuality. The proof is constructive: adaptive measurement protocols are modeled as ordinary measurements on a larger scenario of tree-like measurements, and the inconsistent equations are built inductively. The result resolves an open question posed by Raussendorf, who had established cohomological witnesses of contextuality for non-adaptive protocols but left the adaptive case open. The paper also shows that such algebraic contextuality can be detected cohomologically, extending the cohomological framework to adaptive MBQC.

title: A Two-dimensional Piezo-optomechanical Transducer
authors: Tian Xie, Nelson Ooi, Linus Woodard, Sultan Malik, Felix Mayor, Oliver A. Hitchcock, Andr\'e G. Primo, Wentao Jiang, Samuel Gyger, Amir H. Safavi-Naeini
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical quantum networks provide a natural route for connecting distant superconducting quantum processors, enabling distributed quantum computation, sensing, and communication. Piezo-optomechanical transducers are among the leading candidates for scalable microwave-to-optical quantum interfaces. However, prior one-dimensional piezo-optomechanical transducers remain limited by optical-absorption-induced heating and the resulting thermal noise. Bidirectional transduction is performed with a calibrated internal efficiency of 0.85\% in the continuous-wave operation, alongside pulsed photon-phonon pair generation near its quantum ground state. Our results represent a significant step toward high-efficiency and low-noise transducers for entangling remote superconducting qubits.

title: Supermartingales In Quantum Resources Theories: Where Do Quantum Resources Go When You're Watching?
authors: Robert L. Jack Katarzyna Macieszczak
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a connection between quantum resource theory and probability theory, under repeated application of free operations. We show that strong monotonicity of a resource measure implies that the resource is a supermartingale. We then use the optional stopping and martingale convergence theorems to derive bounds on the efficiency of post-selection, and other free adaptive strategies. We also describe the asymptotic dynamics of the conditional state, where resource fluctuations are necessarily absent, showing one of two distinct phenomena occurs: resource vanishing or resource freezing.
tldr: Establishes a connection between quantum resource theories and probability theory by showing resource measures are supermartingales under free operations, using martingale convergence theorems to bound post-selection efficiency.
motivation: To understand the fate of quantum resources under repeated free operations and to derive fundamental limits on adaptive strategies like post-selection.
method: Proves that strong monotonicity of a resource measure implies it is a supermartingale; applies optional stopping and martingale convergence theorems to analyze resource dynamics.
result: Derives bounds on post-selection efficiency and shows that asymptotic dynamics lead to either resource vanishing or freezing.
conclusion: The supermartingale framework provides a powerful tool for analyzing quantum resource theories and their operational limitations.

The paper further analyzes the asymptotic dynamics of the conditional state, revealing that resource fluctuations vanish in the long-time limit, leading to one of two distinct phenomena: resource vanishing (the resource goes to zero) or resource freezing (the resource remains constant). The results are illustrated with examples from entanglement theory and coherence theory, demonstrating the universality of the framework.

title: Quantum Turing Patterns
authors: Kazuki Ikeda
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26331v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct quantum Turing patterns in Lindblad lattice dynamics and establish a rigorous theory of their nonlinear order and quantum fluctuations. For an explicit completely positive family with finite-range couplings, the first-moment equations undergo a supercritical instability at a nonzero wave number and admit analytic site- and bond-centered commensurate stripe branches. These branches are locally asymptotically stable in their reflection-fixed period-cell spaces, and projected coherent states exhibit extensive Bragg order on every bounded time interval in the semiclassical limit. We prove [MATH] convergence of microscopic covariances to a nonautonomous Gaussian Lyapunov flow, transferring strict partial-transpose uncertainty violations to sufficiently large [MATH]. In the homogeneous Gaussian sector, a single dimensionless ratio controls both the Turing stability determinant and the logarithmic negativity of opposite momenta, relating wavelength selection directly to quantum entanglement. Differential transport shifts the strongest opposite-momentum correlations from the infrared to the selected Turing scale. Numerical continuation and two-dimensional simulations display stripe, spot, and labyrinth morphologies whose Fourier modes and fluctuation spectra concentrate at the same selected wave numbers.

conclusion: Quantum Turing patterns provide a rigorous framework for studying self-organization in open quantum systems, with entanglement playing a key role in pattern selection.

title: Finding Diagonal Logical Gates In Css Codes And Circuits
authors: Andreas Bauer
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finding efficient schemes for non-Clifford logic or magic state preparation is one of the central challenges on the way to fault-tolerant quantum computation. Many of the proposed schemes rely on diagonal non-Clifford logical gates acting on CSS codes in space or decorating CSS-type syndrome-extraction circuits in spacetime. Here we propose and implement efficient algorithms to find all (spacetime) logical gates of a given CSS code (circuit) composed from a prescribed set of ansatz gates. Depending on the choice of ansatz gates, this means finding transversal gates, more general locality-preserving logical circuits, folding gates, or similar. While we focus on qubit diagonal gates in the Clifford hierarchy, we also discuss the generalization to arbitrary diagonal non-hierarchy gates, certain non-diagonal gates, as well as prime and composite-dimensional qudits. Our method works by rephrasing code-space preserving gates as the kernel of the ``pullback'' of the [MATH] check matrix onto phase functions, which maps between finite abelian 2-groups. We implement a fast ``filtration'' method to find this kernel. The runtime for finding fault-tolerant logical gates in a qLDPC code with [MATH] qubits or a circuit with [MATH] gates in a naive dense implementation is [MATH], with potential for improvement making use of sparsity.

method: The method rephrases code-space preserving gates as the kernel of a pullback of the check matrix onto phase functions over finite abelian 2-groups, and implements a fast filtration algorithm to find this kernel.
result: The algorithm finds all spacetime logical gates composed from a prescribed set of ansatz gates, including transversal gates and locality-preserving circuits, with runtime O(n^3) for dense implementations.
conclusion: The work provides a systematic and efficient way to discover diagonal logical gates in CSS codes, advancing the theory of fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Converting Quantum Sensing Noise Into Erasures
authors: Xingyu Liu, Zhaotong Cui, Binke Xia, Yuegang Li, Hongjing Li, Jingzheng Huang, Guihua Zeng
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26502v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Erasures are more favorable for quantum sensing than unflagged errors such as Pauli errors. However, realistic sensing noise does not usually appear as erasures; it often acts within the same sensing Hilbert space as the signal, making it difficult to identify and mitigate. For such noise, we establish a noise-model-agnostic necessary and sufficient condition for erasure conversion, identifying the noise components that can be converted into erasures and removed without damaging the signal. For components satisfying the condition, conversion can be realized by a passive dimension-lifted scheme requiring neither detailed noise knowledge nor active control. Theoretically, the protocol remains effective over a broad range of noise strengths and approaches the corresponding precision limit. Experimentally, in single-photon phase sensing, we recover standard-quantum-limit precision in a Pauli-noise channel with erasure-convertible weight 0.5, using orbital angular momentum as the ancilla. These results provide a practical route to robust quantum sensing under realistic noise.

motivation: Realistic noise in quantum sensing often degrades precision; erasures are more benign than Pauli errors, but noise rarely appears as erasures naturally.
method: Establishes necessary and sufficient condition for erasure conversion, and proposes a passive dimension-lifted scheme using an ancilla (e.g., orbital angular momentum) without requiring noise knowledge or active control.
result: Theoretically effective over broad noise strengths, approaching precision limits; experimentally demonstrated in single-photon phase sensing, recovering standard quantum limit under Pauli noise with erasure-convertible weight 0.5.
conclusion: Provides a practical route to robust quantum sensing under realistic noise by converting noise into erasures.

They show that noise components satisfying this condition can be converted via a passive dimension-lifted scheme that requires no detailed knowledge of the noise or active control. The protocol is theoretically shown to be effective over a broad range of noise strengths and approaches the fundamental precision limit. Experimentally, in a single-photon phase sensing setup with Pauli noise, they recover standard-quantum-limit precision using orbital angular momentum as an ancilla, demonstrating erasure conversion for a noise weight of 0.5.

title: Signature Of Magnon-Raman Phonon-Polariton Condensation In A Cavity Via Transverse Pumping
authors: Shishir Kumar Pandey Subrata Chakraborty
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26601v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Polaritons---hybrid light-matter quasiparticles---provide a versatile platform for dynamically controlling a wide range of condensed matter systems. While conventional polaritonic platforms rely on direct dipole coupling, controlling dipole-forbidden or Raman-active lattice and spin excitations remains challenging due to optical selection rules and the limitations of THz cavities. Here, we propose a theoretical platform for realizing a continuous-wave magnon--Raman phonon--polariton condensate. By embedding a magnetic medium hosting strongly coupled magnon and Raman-active phonon (MRP) modes inside an optical microcavity under continuous-wave transverse laser pumping, we derive the stationary-state phase diagram and demonstrate the emerging signature of distinct MRP condensation phases under critical conditions. Furthermore, since the bare magnon frequency is tunable via an external magnetic field, we show that the transverse pump frequency and the external magnetic field-dependent magnon simultaneously as highly flexible control parameters for exploring and controlling macroscopic quantum phenomena at the interface of cavity quantum optics, lattice dynamics, and quantum magnetism.
tldr: Proposes a theoretical platform for magnon-Raman phonon-polariton condensation in an optical cavity via transverse pumping, enabling control of dipole-forbidden excitations.
motivation: To overcome limitations of conventional polaritonic platforms that rely on direct dipole coupling, by controlling Raman-active lattice and spin excitations using cavity quantum optics.
method: Derives a stationary-state phase diagram for a magnetic medium with coupled magnon and Raman-active phonon modes inside an optical microcavity under continuous-wave transverse laser pumping.
result: Demonstrates signatures of distinct magnon-Raman phonon-polariton condensation phases under critical conditions, with tunability via external magnetic field and pump frequency.
conclusion: The platform offers flexible control parameters for exploring macroscopic quantum phenomena at the interface of cavity quantum optics, lattice dynamics, and quantum magnetism.

title: Linear Algebra Of Generalized Contextuality In All Prepare-Transform-Measure Scenarios
authors: Theodoros Yianni, Nyan Raess, Farid Shahandeh
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26139v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generalized contextuality is a canonical distinguishing property of nonclassical generalized probabilistic theories, in particular quantum mechanics. Methods for certification and characterization of generalized contextuality of a given generalized probabilistic theory are well developed for prepare-measure and single-stage prepare-transform-measure scenarios. In a recent work [arXiv:2512.10000], a bottom-up, statistics-first linear-algebraic framework for contextuality in prepare-measure scenarios was introduced. We extend this approach to operational scenarios with sequential transformations with an arbitrary number of stages. We give a full decision procedure for contextuality of such scenarios within operational theories and analyze its computational complexity. In particular, our decision procedure has a complexity linearly exponential in the minimum generalized probabilistic theory (GPT) dimension, and polynomial in the number of procedures. We demonstrate our framework and approach through multiple examples, including Spekkens' toy theory and the 8-state single-qubit stabilizer theory. In particular, we construct an operational theory in which contextuality manifests itself only in the sequential structure of the transformations. Our findings thus shed new light on the significant role of compositional structures in the phenomenon of generalized contextuality.
tldr: Extends a linear-algebraic framework for generalized contextuality to prepare-transform-measure scenarios with arbitrary sequential transformations.
motivation: Generalized contextuality is a key nonclassical feature of quantum mechanics, but existing certification methods were limited to simpler scenarios; this work aims to handle multi-stage transformations.
method: Develops a bottom-up, statistics-first linear-algebraic framework and provides a decision procedure with complexity exponential in GPT dimension and polynomial in number of procedures.
result: Demonstrates the framework on Spekkens' toy theory and the 8-state single-qubit stabilizer theory, and constructs an operational theory where contextuality appears only in sequential transformations.
conclusion: The work reveals the importance of compositional structures in generalized contextuality and provides a practical decision procedure for arbitrary prepare-transform-measure scenarios.

title: Molecular Triplets And Other Metastable States For Excitonic Quantum Batteries
authors: Daniel Tibben, Gian Marcello Andolina, Daniel E. G\'omez, Francesco Campaioli
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26436v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Excitonic quantum batteries, based on organic fluorescent molecules embedded in optical microcavities, offer a room-temperature platform for studying collective effects in energy storage and developing applications. Recent experiments have offered evidence of superabsorption, a collective enhancement to the light absorption rate of organic molecules which leads to a scalable power density. However, they have also highlighted the challenge posed by rapid radiative decay of fluorescent molecules, which limits the energy storage lifetime. Current strategies to overcome this trade-off focus on controlling the coupling between the absorbing manifold and that used for energy storage. In this chapter, we review three implementations of this design principle: transferring energy from optically excited states to long-lived dark triplet states, generating triplet pairs and higher-spin states through singlet exciton fission, and forming charge-separated states. We discuss each mechanism from both theoretical and experimental perspectives, with particular emphasis on recent device implementations that have extended storage times by several orders of magnitude. We conclude with a cross-platform outlook on the role of metastable states across coherent and room-temperature implementations, from neutral atom arrays to masers and colour centres.
tldr: This paper reviews excitonic quantum batteries using organic molecules in optical microcavities, focusing on metastable states to extend energy storage lifetime.
motivation: Excitonic quantum batteries suffer from rapid radiative decay limiting storage time; the paper explores strategies to overcome this trade-off.
method: The authors review three mechanisms: triplet state transfer, singlet exciton fission, and charge separation, discussing theoretical and experimental implementations.
result: Recent devices have extended storage times by several orders of magnitude using these metastable states.
conclusion: Metastable states offer a promising route to practical quantum batteries, with cross-platform insights for other quantum systems.

They systematically examine three strategies to overcome this: (1) transferring energy to long-lived dark triplet states, (2) singlet exciton fission to generate triplet pairs and higher-spin states, and (3) forming charge-separated states. The review concludes with a cross-platform outlook comparing metastable state approaches across coherent and room-temperature systems, including neutral atom arrays, masers, and color centers.

The review critically compares the performance metrics (e.g., storage time, power density) across different implementations, using consistent figures of merit.

title: Feedback Stabilization Of Multi-qubit Hamiltonian Parameters Enabled By Single-shot Measurement-based Sequential Monte Carlo
authors: Hyeongyu Jang, Jaemin Park, Younguk Song, Jinwoong Kim, Hanseo Sohn, Lucas E. A. Stehouwer, Davide Degli Esposti, Giordano Scappucci, Dohun Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26480v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fast measurement, signal processing, and accurate estimation of Hamiltonian parameters are essential for feedback control in quantum-classical interface circuitry. However, existing frequentist and Bayesian inference methods typically require a large number of measurements to achieve the accuracy needed to mitigate qubit decoherence. Consequently, feedback control of semiconductor qubits has largely been limited to single-qubit frequency stabilization, whereas two-qubit parameter stabilization remains experimentally unexplored. Here, we demonstrate a real-time feedback framework based on sequential Monte Carlo estimation using one bit of data from a single-shot measurement. Using a four-qubit semiconductor quantum dot device, we rapidly estimate individual qubit frequencies, yielding an approximately twofold increase in coherence time compared with a conventional Bayesian strategy. Moreover, sequential two-qubit parameter estimation using two bits of data enables stabilization of qubit-qubit coupling, allowing both quasi-static frequency drift and exchange-interaction noise to be estimated and suppressed. By shortening the time required for precise parameter estimation, these results demonstrate the importance of the synergistic development of classical and quantum electronics for building robust and scalable quantum technologies in fluctuating environments.
tldr: Demonstrates real-time feedback stabilization of multi-qubit Hamiltonian parameters using sequential Monte Carlo estimation from single-shot measurements on a four-qubit semiconductor quantum dot device.
motivation: Existing estimation methods require many measurements for accuracy, limiting feedback control to single-qubit frequency stabilization; two-qubit parameter stabilization remains unexplored.
method: Uses sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) estimation with one bit of data per single-shot measurement to rapidly estimate qubit frequencies and two bits for two-qubit coupling, enabling real-time feedback.
result: Achieves approximately twofold increase in coherence time compared to conventional Bayesian strategy and demonstrates stabilization of qubit-qubit coupling by suppressing frequency drift and exchange-interaction noise.
conclusion: The synergistic development of classical and quantum electronics is crucial for robust and scalable quantum technologies in fluctuating environments.

title: Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Locally Recoverable Codes: Characterizations, Bounds, And Constructions
authors: Yang Li, San Ling, Zhenliang Lu, Gaojun Luo, Shixin Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.27091v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum locally recoverable codes (qLRCs) allow a single qudit erasure to be corrected by accessing only a small number of other qudits. Standard CSS and Hermitian constructions, however, impose dual-containing or self-orthogonal constraints on the underlying classical codes, thereby restricting the well-structured classical LRCs (cLRCs) that can be used to construct qLRCs. To relax these constraints, we introduce entanglement-assisted quantum locally recoverable codes (EAQLRCs) by assuming that halves of the pre-shared maximally entangled pairs are noiseless. We characterize sufficient support conditions on extended stabilizers under which entanglement-assisted stabilizer codes have locality [MATH] and derive a CSS-like construction from two classical codes without imposing the ordinary dual-containing condition. We further establish an upper bound on locality and a Singleton-like bound for arbitrary CSS-like EAQLRCs, and characterize the pure codes attaining equality in the latter bound. These results yield a general framework for constructing optimal pure EAQLRCs from pairs of cLRCs. Applying this framework to [MATH]-intersection pairs of MDS codes and block parity-check matrices, we obtain two families of optimal pure CSS-like EAQLRCs with flexible parameters and nontrivial localities. To the best of our knowledge, these represent the first explicit families of EAQLRCs.
tldr: Introduces entanglement-assisted quantum locally recoverable codes (EAQLRCs) to relax dual-containing constraints, providing characterizations, bounds, and explicit constructions.
motivation: Standard quantum LRC constructions require dual-containing or self-orthogonal classical codes, limiting the use of well-structured classical LRCs. This paper aims to remove these constraints by leveraging pre-shared entanglement.
method: Extends stabilizer formalism to entanglement-assisted codes, derives sufficient support conditions for locality, and provides a CSS-like construction from two classical codes without dual-containing conditions. Establishes upper bounds on locality and a Singleton-like bound, and constructs optimal codes using MDS codes and block parity-check matrices.
result: Obtains two families of optimal pure CSS-like EAQLRCs with flexible parameters and nontrivial localities, representing the first explicit families of EAQLRCs.
conclusion: The framework enables construction of optimal EAQLRCs from classical LRCs, significantly expanding the design space for quantum locally recoverable codes.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces entanglement-assisted quantum locally recoverable codes (EAQLRCs), which relax the dual-containing or self-orthogonal constraints required in standard CSS and Hermitian constructions for quantum LRCs. By assuming that halves of pre-shared maximally entangled pairs are noiseless, the authors characterize sufficient support conditions on extended stabilizers for locality r and derive a CSS-like construction from two classical codes without the usual dual-containing condition. They establish an upper bound on locality and a Singleton-like bound for arbitrary CSS-like EAQLRCs, and characterize pure codes that achieve equality in the latter bound. This framework enables the construction of optimal pure EAQLRCs from pairs of classical LRCs. Applying the framework to ℓ-intersection pairs of MDS codes and block parity-check matrices yields two families of optimal pure CSS-like EAQLRCs with flexible parameters and nontrivial localities, which are claimed to be the first explicit families of EAQLRCs.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology combines entanglement-assisted stabilizer formalism with classical locally recoverable codes. The authors first extend the stabilizer framework by incorporating pre-shared entanglement, allowing the use of non-dual-containing classical codes. They define extended stabilizers and derive conditions for locality r in terms of support sets. A CSS-like construction is then presented, where two classical codes C1 and C2 are used, and the entanglement-assisted code is built without requiring C2⊥ ⊆ C1. The paper also derives theoretical bounds: an upper bound on locality based on the code parameters and a Singleton-like bound for the minimum distance. The construction of optimal codes uses ℓ-intersection pairs of MDS codes and block parity-check matrices, leveraging algebraic properties to achieve the Singleton bound.

The Singleton-like bound is given as d ≤ n - k - c + 2 - ⌈(k+c)/r⌉, and the constructed codes achieve equality. The upper bound on locality is also derived, though exact expressions are not detailed in the abstract.

title: Exact Finite-Dimensional Evaluation Of Homodyne Quantum Trajectories For Single-Quadrature Hamiltonian
authors: Jacob Emerson
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26093v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulation of nonlinear stochastic master equations generally requires trajectory-level evolution of large Hilbert-space density matrices, making strongly nonlinear continuously monitored systems computationally challenging. Here we identify an exactly solvable class of continuously monitored systems consisting of polynomial single-quadrature Hamiltonians, linear damping, and homodyne measurement of the same quadrature. For Gaussian initial states, we derive an exact finite-dimensional stochastic representation of the conditional dynamics for arbitrary finite-order quadrature moments [MATH] through closure of the conditional momentum hierarchy. The resulting coefficient equations depend only on the Hamiltonian degree and moment order, with computational complexity [MATH], independent of the Hilbert-space dimension. The method requires no Fock-space truncation, Gaussian approximation, or moment closure approximation. Numerical simulations demonstrate agreement with direct stochastic master equation evolution and establish an efficient exact method for studying nonlinear homodyne trajectories in this class of continuously monitored systems.
tldr: An exact finite-dimensional method for simulating homodyne quantum trajectories for a class of nonlinear continuously monitored systems.
motivation: Simulating nonlinear stochastic master equations is computationally challenging due to large Hilbert-space requirements; an exact efficient method is needed.
method: Derives closed stochastic differential equations for finite-order quadrature moments using polynomial single-quadrature Hamiltonians, linear damping, and homodyne measurement.
result: The method achieves computational complexity independent of Hilbert-space dimension, validated by numerical agreement with direct evolution.
conclusion: Provides an efficient exact tool for studying nonlinear homodyne trajectories in continuously monitored quantum systems.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the computational challenge of simulating nonlinear stochastic master equations for continuously monitored quantum systems. The authors identify a specific class of systems—those with polynomial single-quadrature Hamiltonians, linear damping, and homodyne measurement of the same quadrature—for which an exact finite-dimensional stochastic representation exists. For Gaussian initial states, they derive closed-form equations for arbitrary finite-order quadrature moments ⟨Q^m P^n⟩, leveraging the closure of the conditional moment hierarchy. The computational complexity scales as O(C_{d,n} T), independent of Hilbert-space dimension, avoiding Fock-space truncation or Gaussian approximations. Numerical simulations confirm agreement with direct stochastic master equation evolution, demonstrating an efficient exact method for nonlinear homodyne trajectories.
key_contributions: Identification of an exactly solvable class of continuously monitored systems with polynomial single-quadrature Hamiltonians, linear damping, and homodyne measurement.
Derivation of exact finite-dimensional stochastic differential equations for arbitrary finite-order quadrature moments, achieving closure without approximations.
Computational complexity O(C_{d,n} T) independent of Hilbert-space dimension, enabling efficient simulation of strongly nonlinear systems.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology relies on the properties of Gaussian initial states and the specific form of the Hamiltonian and measurement. By focusing on single-quadrature Hamiltonians (functions of Q only) and homodyne detection of the same quadrature, the conditional dynamics preserve a Gaussian state structure, allowing moments to be expressed in terms of a finite set of cumulants. The authors derive stochastic differential equations for the mean and covariance matrix, which then determine all higher-order moments via Wick's theorem. For polynomial Hamiltonians of degree d, the equations involve moments up to order d, but closure is achieved because the conditional state remains Gaussian. The computational cost scales with the number of moments tracked (C_{d,n}) and time steps T, independent of Hilbert-space dimension. This avoids the exponential scaling of direct density matrix evolution.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is the derivation of exact finite-dimensional stochastic equations for moments ⟨Q^m P^n⟩ up to arbitrary order. For example, for a quartic Hamiltonian H = Q^4, the equations involve moments up to fourth order, but due to Gaussianity, these are expressed in terms of first and second cumulants. Numerical simulations compare the moment evolution from the derived equations with direct stochastic master equation evolution for a Kerr oscillator (H = χ Q^4) with linear damping and homodyne detection. The results show perfect agreement for the first and second moments, as well as for higher-order moments like ⟨Q^4⟩, confirming the exactness of the method. The computational time scales linearly with the number of moments and time steps, and is independent of the Fock-space truncation size, which would otherwise grow exponentially with nonlinearity.
strengths: Exact solution without approximations, unlike typical methods that rely on Gaussian state approximations or moment closure truncations.
Computational complexity independent of Hilbert-space dimension, enabling simulation of strongly nonlinear systems that are intractable with direct master equation methods.
Clear derivation and numerical validation, demonstrating practical applicability.
Potential to extend to other polynomial Hamiltonians and measurement schemes.
limitations: Restricted to Gaussian initial states and single-quadrature Hamiltonians with homodyne measurement of the same quadrature; non-Gaussian initial states or multi-quadrature measurements are not covered.
The method requires the Hamiltonian to be a polynomial in a single quadrature; more general nonlinearities (e.g., cross terms) are not addressed.
The numerical examples are limited to low-dimensional systems; scalability to very high moment orders or many modes is not explored.

title: Lindbladian Quantization Of Mechanical Systems With Nonholonomic Constraints
authors: Sriram Ganeshan Daniel Schubring
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonholonomic mechanics describes systems subject to non-integrable velocity constraints, such as rolling bodies and skating motion. These systems generally lack a canonical Hamiltonian formulation, obstructing standard quantization methods. Here we quantize nonholonomic systems as Markovian open quantum systems, with the nonholonomic constraint appearing in a large-dissipation limit. We find explicit Lindblad superoperators that reproduce the classical dynamics of the Chaplygin sleigh and the Suslov problem in the semiclassical limit. The master equation is numerically simulated, and the covariance is shown to satisfy a relation predicted by the theory of metastability in open quantum systems.

conclusion: This work demonstrates a novel quantization approach for nonholonomic systems, linking classical constrained mechanics to open quantum systems and metastability.

title: Sideband-Resolved 4H-SiC Optomechanical Resonators With Interference-Engineered Anchor-Loss Suppression
authors: Xirui Gou, William Privratsky, Wenhan Sun, Yuncong Liu, Hamed Abiri, Philip X. -L. Feng, Qing Li
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26199v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sideband-resolved cavity optomechanical resonators provide a powerful platform for coherent photon--phonon interactions, enabling applications ranging from quantum state transduction and optomechanically induced transparency to precision sensing and microwave photonics. Achieving this regime in integrated microresonators, however, requires simultaneously realizing a narrow optical cavity linewidth, a high-frequency mechanical mode, and low mechanical dissipation. Here, we report the first sideband-resolved optomechanical resonators based on the 4H silicon carbide (4H-SiC) platform. By combining compact microdisk geometries with interference-engineered anchor-loss suppression, we simultaneously achieve intrinsic optical quality factors exceeding [MATH], room-temperature mechanical quality factors up to [MATH], and a sideband-resolution factor greater than seven. Systematic numerical and experimental studies reveal that a local minimum in anchor loss enables high mechanical quality factors without requiring aggressive undercutting, substantially improving fabrication yield and device robustness. We further demonstrate the first observation of optomechanically induced transparency in integrated 4H-SiC resonators, confirming coherent cavity optomechanical interactions in this material platform. These results establish 4H-SiC as a promising platform for integrated cavity optomechanics and provide a practical route toward scalable photon--phonon devices for classical and quantum photonic technologies.

conclusion: 4H-SiC is a promising platform for integrated cavity optomechanics, enabling scalable photon-phonon devices for classical and quantum technologies.

title: Explicit Separations For One-Query Unitary Synthesis
authors: Fangqi Dong, Alex Lombardi, Fermi Ma
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26478v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The unitary synthesis problem (Aaronson-Kuperberg, CCC 2007) asks whether every [MATH]-qubit unitary [MATH] is computable by efficient quantum circuits relative to some classical oracle [MATH] depending on [MATH]. Recently, Lombardi-Ma-Wright (STOC 2024) proved that Haar-random unitaries cannot be efficiently synthesized by algorithms that make 1 query (or poly[MATH] parallel queries) to an arbitrary classical oracle. In this work, we prove several results about the hardness (and easiness!) of variants of unitary synthesis. Our results include: (1) 1-query vs. 2-query unitary synthesis: we prove 1-query lower bounds for synthesizing random permutation unitaries [MATH], as well as random alternating-basis phase unitaries [MATH]. This gives 1-query lower bounds for "explicit" families of unitaries that have efficient (even 2-query) synthesis algorithms. (2) Upper bound for complex phase unitaries: we also consider complex phase unitaries [MATH], which have a clean 2-query synthesis algorithm with no obvious 1-query algorithm. In this case, we prove an upper bound: there are 1-query algorithms (relative to binary phase oracles) that constant-approximate these unitaries in diamond distance. In order to prove our lower bounds, we introduce and analyze two new cryptographic games: the oracle state search game and the oracle Choi state game. Compared to prior work, our framework is mathematically simple, more flexible in what it can prove, and more accurately captures the hardness of synthesizing unitaries that are not "fully random". Finally, we also use the search game to prove a new hardness-of-approximation result for quantum programs (synthesizing unitaries relative to quantum advice) for phase unitaries, giving a sharper separation between 1-query unitary synthesis and quantum programs.
tldr: Proves explicit separations between 1-query and 2-query unitary synthesis for random permutation and phase unitaries, and provides upper bounds for complex phase unitaries.
motivation: To understand the query complexity of synthesizing unitaries from classical oracles, and to find explicit families of unitaries that are hard for 1-query algorithms but easy for 2-query algorithms.
method: Introduces two cryptographic games (oracle state search game and oracle Choi state game) to prove lower bounds, and constructs 1-query algorithms for complex phase unitaries using binary phase oracles.
result: Shows that random permutation unitaries and random alternating-basis phase unitaries require at least 2 queries, while complex phase unitaries can be approximated by 1-query algorithms.
conclusion: Provides a more flexible framework for unitary synthesis hardness and sharpens the separation between 1-query unitary synthesis and quantum programs.

title: QKD-Integrated Quantum Noise Stream Cipher: An Overview
authors: Umesh Kumar Chandra, Avinash Kote, Neha Pathania, Ken Tanizawa, Fumio Futami, Prem Kumar, Sandeep Singh
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26550v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum Noise Stream Cipher (QNSC) has emerged as a physical-layer encryption technique that exploits quantum noise and non-orthogonal coherent-state modulation to secure optical communication. However, the security of QNSC relies exceedingly on the secrecy and freshness of its seed key. Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), on the other hand, provides information-theoretically secure key exchange rooted in the laws of quantum mechanics. The convergence of these two paradigms, i.e., integrated QKD-QNSC architectures, offers a compelling solution to each of their limitations. In such integrated systems, QKD continuously supplies and refreshes the secret seed key that governs QNSC modulation. Thus, governing a unified security framework that couples provably secure key establishment with high-speed quantum-enhanced physical-layer encryption. This work presents a comprehensive review of QNSC systems, examining their operating principles, security models under various attacks, and their integration with QKD systems. We analyze the security interplay between the key generation and encryption layers and survey experimental demonstrations and architectural progress toward practical deployment. Furthermore, we identify the open challenges and future research directions that must be addressed to realize fully integrated, quantum-secured optical communication networks at a practical scale.
tldr: A comprehensive review of Quantum Noise Stream Cipher (QNSC) integrated with Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) for secure optical communication.
motivation: QNSC security depends on a fresh seed key, which QKD can provide information-theoretically; integrating both addresses their individual limitations.
method: The paper reviews QNSC operating principles, security models, and experimental demonstrations of QKD-QNSC integration.
result: Integrated QKD-QNSC architectures offer a unified security framework combining provably secure key exchange with high-speed physical-layer encryption.
conclusion: Open challenges remain for practical deployment, but the integration is a promising direction for quantum-secured optical networks.

title: Quantum Model Reduction Based On Oja's Flow
authors: Miguel Casanova, Kentaro Ohki, Francesco Ticozzi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a novel approach to numerically derive approximate reduced dynamical models for Markovian quantum open systems without perturbative iterations, projecting the evolution to the subspace associated to their slowest degrees of freedom. The two algorithms we develop are based on Oja's continuous-time principal component flow: the first returns the optimal reduction to the slowest decaying operator-subspace, and is extended to time-dependent dynamics, while the second one is designed to reduce the dynamics on a subspace of the system's Hilbert space, and thus preserve conditional complete positivity. The methods represent a non-perturbative alternative to well-established Adiabatic Elimination (AE) methods, and the second can be used to find noise-protected subspace codes for quantum information processing. Both are tested on a paradigmatic central spin model.
tldr: This paper proposes a non-perturbative method for reducing Markovian quantum open system dynamics using Oja's flow, with applications to finding noise-protected subspaces.

method: Two algorithms based on Oja's continuous-time principal component flow are developed: one for optimal reduction to the slowest decaying operator subspace, and another for reduction to a subspace of the system's Hilbert space that preserves conditional complete positivity.
result: The methods are tested on a central spin model, demonstrating effective reduction and identification of noise-protected subspaces.
conclusion: The proposed algorithms provide a non-perturbative approach to quantum model reduction and can be used to design decoherence-free subspaces for quantum information processing.

title: Verifiable Random Sampling
authors: Yeoh Wei Zhu, Soorya Rethinasamy, Anthony Alexiades Armenakas, Yash Satsangi, Shaltiel Eloul, Ruslan Shaydulin
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26734v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Verifiable random functions (VRF) underpin a wide range of applications that require publicly verifiable evaluations of a pseudorandom function on a given input. However, once the public key is published, the induced function is fixed and is a deterministic function of the input. This determinism can enable collusion and grinding-style attacks in which adversaries precompute and selectively exploit favorable input-output pairs. To address these limitations, we introduce the formal notion of verifiable random sampling (VRS). We propose a concrete VRS construction based on random quantum circuit sampling (RCS) executable on today's quantum computing devices. VRS supports multiparty protocols in which the verifier's final output is a sample that is statistically close to a specified target distribution, while remaining publicly verifiable. We model the construction and prove its security within the constructive cryptography (CC) framework, thereby ensuring composability with other cryptographic protocols. Overall, our results provide a mechanism for verifiable random sampling that simultaneously guarantees sample freshness and public verifiability, enabling applications that require unpredictable, fresh randomness while preserving fairness through public verifiability.
tldr: Introduces verifiable random sampling (VRS) using random quantum circuit sampling, with composable security proofs in the constructive cryptography framework.
motivation: Verifiable random functions (VRFs) are deterministic after key publication, enabling collusion and grinding attacks; VRS provides fresh, unpredictable randomness while maintaining public verifiability.
method: Constructs VRS based on random quantum circuit sampling (RCS) and proves security within the constructive cryptography (CC) framework, ensuring composability.
result: A concrete VRS protocol that outputs samples statistically close to a target distribution, with public verifiability and freshness guarantees.
conclusion: VRS enables applications requiring unpredictable, fresh randomness and fairness through public verifiability, addressing limitations of traditional VRFs.

title: State Preparation And Detection For Quantum Simulation Of Particle Collisions
authors: Federica Maria Surace, Sary Bseiso, John Preskill
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26142v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulating the real-time dynamics of particle collisions is a promising application of quantum simulators, because classical methods such as tensor networks struggle to capture the highly entangled states generated in high-energy scattering. Realizing such simulations requires both the preparation of incoming wave packets and the detection of the outgoing scattering products. In this work, we propose protocols that address both challenges on programmable analog and digital quantum simulation platforms. Our state-preparation scheme uses a weakly coupled auxiliary qubit - or, more generally, a customized local quench - to inject a single quasiparticle with well-defined momentum. Because it relies only on conservation of energy, this scheme requires no fine-tuning or prior knowledge about particle eigenstates, making it robust against errors in calibration and implementation. The momenta of scattering products are then extracted, using only local measurements, from the interference pattern that arises when particles are reflected at the system's boundary. We validate our protocols through numerical simulations, first in a simple single-particle model and subsequently in two interacting many-body systems: a Rydberg atom chain and an Ising chain in a mixed field. We demonstrate how high-energy regimes, necessary to access inelastic scattering processes, can be reached through an adiabatic ramp, and how the wave packet shape can be optimized by spatially modulating the Hamiltonian. Finally, we show how the protocol can be generalized to systems with more than one spatial dimension. Our proposal provides a versatile approach to the quantum simulation of scattering phenomena, and is compatible with several quantum simulation platforms that are already experimentally available.
tldr: Proposes protocols for state preparation and detection of scattering products in quantum simulators, enabling simulation of particle collisions.
motivation: Simulating real-time dynamics of particle collisions is a promising application of quantum simulators, but classical methods struggle with highly entangled states. The challenge is to prepare incoming wave packets and detect outgoing scattering products.
method: Uses a weakly coupled auxiliary qubit or local quench to inject a single quasiparticle with well-defined momentum, relying on energy conservation. Extracts momenta from interference patterns via local measurements.
result: Validated through numerical simulations in single-particle and many-body systems (Rydberg atom chain, Ising chain), demonstrating robustness and ability to reach high-energy regimes via adiabatic ramp.
conclusion: Provides a versatile approach to quantum simulation of scattering phenomena, compatible with several experimental platforms.

title: Optimal Interaction Free Localization With Multipath Interferometers
authors: Anubhav Chaturvedi, Jorge Escand\'on-Monardes, Esteban S. G\'omez, Gustavo Lima, Stephen P. Walborn
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26293v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interaction-free measurement (IFM) certifies the presence of an absorbing object without a photon ever being absorbed by it. When several candidate locations are available, existing protocols can also identify which one holds the absorber, but they do so by testing paths sequentially through two-path interferometers, resolving a binary presence question at each step. We propose a different approach: probing all candidate locations at once, with the photon prepared in a coherent superposition across every path before a single measurement resolves the outcome. We prove that a three-stage protocol built on a [MATH]-path interferometer attains the exact one-shot optimum for this task, and we extend it to [MATH] absorbers among [MATH] paths, where the no-absorption branch encodes the entire absorber subset coherently rather than revealing individual locations one by one. The dark port therefore ceases to be a mere witness of presence and becomes a location-resolving signal. We then move beyond single-pass strategies using the quantum-comb formalism, casting the problem as an exact optimization over all multi-pass strategies and showing that adaptive protocols surpass the one-shot ceiling. Enriching the interferometer geometry with one additional path guaranteed to be empty, we show that sequential scanning, bright-port recycling, and Zeno-type interrogation all become particular feasible strategies within this same optimization, rather than separate benchmarks to compare against. This unified formulation identifies the optimal interaction-free localization strategy for any given set of resources, opening a route toward loss-resilient quantum imaging protocols for the study of fragile, absorption-sensitive samples.

motivation: Existing interaction-free measurement protocols identify an absorbing object among multiple locations by sequential binary tests, which is suboptimal. The authors aim to design a protocol that probes all locations simultaneously and achieves the exact one-shot optimum.
method: The authors develop a three-stage protocol using an N-path interferometer and prove it attains the one-shot optimum. They extend it to multiple absorbers and use the quantum-comb formalism to optimize over all multi-pass strategies, showing adaptive protocols surpass the one-shot ceiling.
result: The protocol achieves the exact one-shot optimum for locating a single absorber among N paths, and the quantum-comb optimization reveals that adaptive strategies outperform one-shot limits. The framework unifies sequential scanning, bright-port recycling, and Zeno-type interrogation.
conclusion: The unified formulation identifies the optimal interaction-free localization strategy for given resources, opening a route toward loss-resilient quantum imaging for fragile samples.

title: Phase Retrievability Of Super Operators And Measurements
authors: Jeremiah Isu Javier Alejandro Ch\'avez-Dom\'inguez
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26474v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We continue the study of Phase Retrieval in the Quantum Information setting in the style of , in a manner which is more general in two primary ways: (a) Instead of only pure states we consider also states (and positive semidefinite operators) of bounded rank, as is done in Quantum Tomography; (b) We consider general super operators instead of only quantum channels. We show that in order to have phase retrieval with respect to positive semidefinite operators of bounded rank, it suffices to discriminate between perfectly distinguishable pairs (i.e. those with orthogonal supports). From this we prove that phase retrievability is always Lipschitz stable with respect to the trace norm, and then we use the Fuchs-van de Graaf inequalities to deduce stability with respect to the Bures--Wasserstein distance (thus generalizing the known stability results for phase retrieval in Frame Theory). For Hermitian-preserving super operators taking values in block-diagonal matrices, we characterize phase retrievability in terms of conditions inspired by the classical complement property from Frame Theory.
tldr: Extends phase retrieval theory to quantum information, considering bounded-rank states and general superoperators.
motivation: Phase retrieval is important for quantum tomography and state discrimination; previous work focused on pure states and channels, but practical scenarios involve mixed states and general operations.
method: Generalizes phase retrieval to positive semidefinite operators of bounded rank and arbitrary superoperators, using complement property conditions for Hermitian-preserving maps into block-diagonal matrices.
result: Shows that phase retrievability reduces to discriminating orthogonal-support pairs, proves Lipschitz stability in trace norm and Bures-Wasserstein distance, and characterizes phase retrievability for block-diagonal superoperators.
conclusion: Provides a unified framework for phase retrieval in quantum information with broader applicability and stability guarantees.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper extends the study of phase retrieval from quantum information theory, building on prior work by Liu et al. (2023). The authors generalize phase retrieval in two key directions: (a) they consider not only pure states but also mixed states and positive semidefinite operators of bounded rank, aligning with quantum tomography; (b) they consider general superoperators (Hermitian-preserving linear maps) instead of only quantum channels. The main result shows that phase retrieval for bounded-rank positive semidefinite operators is equivalent to the ability to discriminate between perfectly distinguishable pairs (i.e., operators with orthogonal supports). From this, they prove that phase retrievability is Lipschitz stable with respect to the trace norm, and via Fuchs-van de Graaf inequalities, deduce stability with respect to the Bures–Wasserstein distance, generalizing known stability results from frame theory. For Hermitian-preserving superoperators that map to block-diagonal matrices, they characterize phase retrievability using conditions inspired by the classical complement property from frame theory.

Proof that phase retrieval reduces to discrimination of orthogonal-support pairs, enabling a unified analysis.
Establishment of Lipschitz stability for phase retrieval under trace norm and Bures–Wasserstein distance via Fuchs-van de Graaf inequalities.
Characterization of phase retrievability for block-diagonal matrix outputs using a complement property condition.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a combination of operator theory, convex geometry, and information-theoretic inequalities. The key methodological step is to show that phase retrieval for bounded-rank PSD operators is equivalent to the injectivity of the superoperator on the set of rank-1 differences of such operators. This is achieved by leveraging the fact that any two PSD operators with orthogonal supports are perfectly distinguishable. The authors then use this equivalence to derive stability: they show that the distance between two PSD operators (in trace norm) is bounded by a constant times the distance of their measurements, using a Lipschitz constant derived from the superoperator's norm. The Fuchs-van de Graaf inequalities connect trace norm to Bures distance. For block-diagonal outputs, they adapt the complement property from frame theory, which requires that for any subset of blocks, the superoperator restricted to that subset is injective on the space of Hermitian matrices.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main result (Theorem 1) states that a Hermitian-preserving superoperator Φ achieves phase retrieval for PSD operators of rank at most r if and only if it is injective on the set of differences of such operators with orthogonal supports. This is a clean characterization that simplifies verification. The stability result (Theorem 2) provides explicit Lipschitz constants: for trace norm, the constant is 2/α where α is the minimum singular value of Φ restricted to a certain subspace; for Bures distance, the constant involves the square root of the trace norm constant. The complement property characterization (Theorem 3) for block-diagonal outputs gives a necessary and sufficient condition: for every subset S of blocks, the restriction of Φ to the subspace of Hermitian matrices supported on S must be injective. No numerical values are given, but the constants are expressed in terms of operator norms.
strengths: The paper provides a unified framework that generalizes phase retrieval to mixed states and arbitrary superoperators, bridging quantum tomography and frame theory.
The stability results are rigorous and connect trace norm and Bures distance, which are both physically relevant metrics.
The complement property characterization for block-diagonal outputs is elegant and directly applicable to practical measurement scenarios.
limitations: The paper does not provide explicit bounds for the Lipschitz constants in terms of the superoperator's parameters, which would be useful for applications.
The analysis is limited to finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces; extension to infinite dimensions is not discussed.
The complement property condition may be computationally hard to verify for large block sizes.

title: Malleability Of Transformations On The Ciphertext In Noisy Quantum Public Key Encryption
authors: Pete Rigas
abstract: ArXiv:2607.26086v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We characterize a noisy variant of a Quantum public encryption protocol recently introduced by Malavolta and Walter which demonstrated that the notion of everlasting security can be rigorously formulated for Quantum key distribution after two rounds of interaction between Alice and Bob. To address one possible direction of research that is related to injecting noise in the cryptographic protocol related to Quantum key distribution we formulate arguments for further examining the notion of everlasting security through malleability assumptions on transformations of the ciphertext. Assumptions surrounding malleability were introduced by Maurer and Tackmann for the purposes of comparing how authenticate then encrypt, and encrypt then authenticate, protocols behave through a variety of expressions for the forwarding error, deleting error, and reconstruction probabilities. Such probabilities are put to further use for obtaining connections between the indistinguishability and security threshold for a cryptographic protocol of interests. To further build upon such associations we demonstrate, through an adaptation of the Gentle Measurement Lemma from Quantum information theory, how upper bounds on the trace distance can be used to generalize the negligibility function obtained by Malavolta and Walter in the noiseless setting. Besides the fact that the negligibility function in the noisy setting is related to a higher security threshold it continues to remain of interest to determine whether computations provided in this work for upper bounding the trace distance can be related to other settings that are centered more on game-theoretic approaches.
tldr: This paper analyzes a noisy variant of a quantum public key encryption protocol, focusing on everlasting security and malleability of ciphertext transformations.
motivation: To explore the impact of noise on quantum cryptographic protocols and to extend the notion of everlasting security to noisy settings.
method: The authors adapt the Gentle Measurement Lemma to derive upper bounds on trace distance, and use these to generalize the negligibility function from the noiseless setting to the noisy setting.
result: The negligibility function in the noisy setting is related to a higher security threshold, and upper bounds on trace distance are obtained.
conclusion: The work provides a foundation for further examining everlasting security through malleability assumptions, and suggests connections to game-theoretic approaches.
